North Dakota law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there.

What the official sources say

  • Title vests in a person in actual, open, adverse and undisputed possession of the land under title (color of title) for ten years who has paid all taxes and assessments legally levied on it. (N.D.C.C. 47-06-03; source)
  • No action to recover real property may be maintained unless the plaintiff or predecessor was seized or possessed of it within twenty years before the action. (N.D.C.C. 28-01-04; source)
  • The holder of legal title is presumed to have been in possession, and another's occupation is presumed subordinate to that title, unless the premises were held adversely for twenty years. (N.D.C.C. 28-01-07; source)
  • An occupant claiming under a written instrument, judgment or decree with continued possession for twenty years is deemed to hold adversely; land counts as occupied if cultivated or improved, substantially enclosed, or used for fuel or fencing timber. (N.D.C.C. 28-01-08 and 28-01-09; source)
  • An eviction action in district court lies where a party enters by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth on another's prior actual possession and detains it, or unlawfully holds possession by force or threats. (N.D.C.C. 47-32-01; source)

North Dakota statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • Security deposit limited to one month's rent, with up to two months allowed for a tenant with a felony conviction or a prior judgment for violating a rental agreement; pet deposit may not exceed the greater of $2,500 or two months' rent. (N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.1; source)
  • Landlord must deliver an itemization of deductions and any refund within thirty days after termination of the lease and delivery of possession; deposit must be held in a federally insured interest-bearing account. (N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.1; source)
  • On transfer of ownership of the rental, the security deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to the new owner; the seller is not relieved of liability until it is transferred. (N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.1; source)
  • Month-to-month tenancy may be ended by either party with at least one calendar month's written notice unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing. (N.D.C.C. 47-16-15; source)
  • Landlord may enter at any time in an emergency; otherwise only at reasonable hours and in a reasonable manner, after notifying the tenant and seeking consent identifying a time certain unless impractical; entry to show the unit to purchasers is allowed. (N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.3; source)
  • Residential landlord must comply with building and housing codes affecting health and safety, keep premises fit and habitable, and maintain electrical, plumbing, heating and other supplied facilities, allowing a reasonable time to remedy. (N.D.C.C. 47-16-13.1; source)
  • If a landlord changes lease terms under 47-16-07, the tenant may terminate at month end with at least twenty-five days' notice. (N.D.C.C. 47-16-13.1 and 47-16-15; source)

What North Dakota rental rules matter when you sell a rented house?

The rules that matter most are the security deposit statute, the notice rules for ending a tenancy, the limits on landlord entry, and the eviction procedure. All of them sit in chapter 47-16 and chapter 47-32 of the North Dakota Century Code. A landlord who plans to sell a house with a tenant in it needs to handle each one correctly, whether the buyer wants the tenant to stay or wants a vacant house.

This guide summarizes the statutes. It is general information and not legal advice, so a landlord with a dispute in progress should talk to a North Dakota attorney.

How do North Dakota security deposit rules work?

A North Dakota landlord may generally collect a deposit of up to one month's rent, and the landlord must hold it in a federally insured, interest-bearing account for the tenant's benefit. The deductions and the return deadline are tightly set, and getting them wrong can cost a landlord triple the amount wrongly kept.

TopicRuleStatute
Deposit capOne month's rent, with exceptions for a tenant with a felony conviction or a prior judgment for violating a rental agreement47-16-07.1
Pet depositNo more than the greater of $2,500 or two months' rent; not for service or companion animals47-16-07.1
Return deadlineItemized deductions and any balance within 30 days after the lease ends and possession is delivered47-16-07.1
InterestNot required if the tenant lived there less than nine months47-16-07.1
Wrongful withholdingExposes the landlord to treble damages47-16-07.1

The Attorney General's tenant page adds that deductions may cover damage or unpaid rent but not normal wear and tear. When a rental is sold, the deposit is a liability that has to be dealt with in the closing paperwork, so ask your title company how the deposit and interest will move to the new owner.

What is the move-in condition statement?

The landlord must give the tenant a written statement describing the property's facilities and condition when the rental agreement begins, and both parties sign it. Under N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.2 it serves as prima facie proof of the condition on that date.

The Attorney General warns tenants to check the report before signing, because a tenant is presumed responsible for damage that is not listed. For a landlord preparing to sell, the signed statement is also the best record of what the house looked like when the tenant arrived. Keep a copy with the lease so a buyer and the title company can see it.

When can a landlord enter to show the house to buyers?

A landlord may enter at reasonable hours and in a reasonable manner for listed purposes, and showings to purchasers are among them. Section 47-16-07.3 also allows entry at any time in an emergency, or when the landlord reasonably believes the tenant has abandoned the unit or is in substantial violation of the lease.

  • Unless it is impractical, the landlord must notify the tenant and ask for consent that identifies a specific time.
  • Consent cannot be unreasonably withheld, and it is presumed if the tenant does not object after notice of a time certain.
  • Using access rights to harass or intimidate a tenant is prohibited.

Plan showings around the tenant's schedule and put the notice in writing. A string of unannounced visits can turn a cooperative tenant into a difficult one.

How can a tenancy be ended when a landlord sells?

Selling a house does not by itself end a lease, so the way to end a tenancy depends on the type of tenancy. For a month-to-month tenancy, either side can end it with at least one calendar month's written notice given at any time, and rent is due through the termination date. For a tenancy with no stated term, notice must be at least as long as the lease period, up to one calendar month.

A landlord who wants to change the terms of a month-to-month tenancy must give written notice at least 30 days before the end of the month, and the change takes effect if the tenant stays. A tenant who does not accept the change may end the tenancy at the end of the month with at least 25 days' notice.

A lease that requires notice longer than one month must say so and include a space for the tenant's initials. Without the initials, the tenant may end the tenancy on the last day of a month with one calendar month's notice.

What must a North Dakota landlord keep in working order?

A residential landlord must comply with the building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, keep the unit fit and habitable, and keep common areas clean and safe. Section 47-16-13.1 also requires waste removal, running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat, with listed exceptions, and the landlord gets a reasonable time to fix a problem after being told.

Tenants carry duties too under 47-16-13.2: keep their area clean and safe, dispose of waste, avoid damaging the premises, and avoid disturbing neighbors. A tenant may end the lease early under 47-16-17 if the landlord fails to make repairs within a reasonable time after a request, and a landlord may end it under 47-16-16 if the tenant uses the property contrary to the agreement.

The Attorney General's office says it cannot take complaints about landlord and tenant disputes or mediate them. Tenants are pointed to Legal Services of North Dakota, a private attorney or small claims court, and discrimination complaints go to the North Dakota Department of Labor.

How does eviction work in North Dakota?

Eviction in North Dakota is a court action, and a landlord cannot remove a tenant without a court order from a district court. The grounds are listed in N.D.C.C. 47-32-01, and the main ones for a rental are listed below.

  • Holding over after the lease ends, or failing to pay rent within three days after it is due.
  • Unreasonably disturbing other tenants' peaceful enjoyment.
  • Materially violating the written lease.
  • Remaining after a foreclosure sale, deed or cancelled contract for deed once the redemption time has expired.

For holdover, nonpayment, foreclosure-related and lease-violation cases the landlord must give three days' written notice of intent to evict before filing. The court summons sets an appearance date between 3 and 15 days after it is issued. If the landlord wins, the judgment is for immediate restitution of the premises, although the court may stay enforcement up to five days when immediate removal would cause substantial hardship.

The Attorney General's page is direct about what a landlord may not do: lock a tenant out, cut off utilities or take belongings. The court's self-help page also says that if the property is owned by an LLC or corporation, the published forms cannot be used, and only a North Dakota-licensed lawyer can represent the entity.

What happens to eviction records and unpaid rent?

A claim for accrued rent and damages can be joined with the eviction action, but other claims generally cannot, and a tenant's counterclaims are limited to setoffs against rent or damages. Section 47-32-05 lets a person move to seal an eviction record for nonpayment or property damage seven years after the order is satisfied, if there has been no other eviction in that time.

Since back rent and damages are tied to the landlord's own claim against the tenant, a landlord who sells should settle in the sale contract who keeps the right to collect them.

What should a landlord check before selling a rental in North Dakota?

A short checklist keeps a rental sale clean.

  • Pull the lease, the move-in condition statement and the deposit records.
  • Confirm the deposit is in a federally insured, interest-bearing account and decide how it will transfer.
  • Give written notice before every showing and ask for a specific time.
  • If the buyer wants the house vacant, use the notice rules for the tenancy type, and file for eviction only on a statutory ground.
  • Keep rent payment methods open: a landlord may not charge a fee for accepting cash, a check or a money order for rent.

Tell any buyer up front whether the tenant will stay, because that decides which notice rules apply and how long the process takes.

More questions about North Dakota Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How much can a North Dakota landlord charge for a security deposit?

A landlord can generally charge up to one month's rent. Higher limits apply to a tenant with a felony conviction or a prior judgment for violating a rental agreement, and pet deposits are capped separately at the greater of $2,500 or two months' rent.

How long does a landlord have to return a deposit in North Dakota?

Thirty days. The landlord must deliver an itemized list of deductions and any balance within 30 days after the lease ends and the tenant gives up possession.

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in North Dakota?

At least one calendar month's written notice, from either the landlord or the tenant, given at any time.

Can a landlord show the house to buyers while it is rented?

Yes, within reason. Entry for showings must be at reasonable hours and in a reasonable manner, and the landlord must notify the tenant and seek consent for a specific time unless that is impractical.

Can a North Dakota landlord evict a tenant without going to court?

No. A tenant cannot be evicted without a court order from a North Dakota district court, and lockouts, utility shutoffs and taking belongings are not allowed.
